evals.prompt: Define a color system in 2-3 sentences. Name its layers and what each layer is for.
expected_elements: Three layers: a palette of raw values (per-hue scales), semantic tokens named by purpose, and a per-theme mapping
The palette is the vocabulary; semantic tokens are the contract components consume; the mapping is what changes between themes
Names intent-based token examples (background-surface, text-primary, danger-emphasis)
Mentions the two binding constraints: perceptual-uniform scale construction and a contrast floor

evals.prompt: Why must color scales be generated in OKLCH or LCH rather than sRGB or HSL?
expected_elements: sRGB and HSL are perceptually non-uniform — equal numeric lightness steps produce unequal perceived changes
Names cliffs around yellow and teal as a symptom
OKLCH and CIELAB are perceptually uniform — equal L steps look equal regardless of hue
This makes them the correct space for generating evenly-stepped scales

evals.prompt: What contrast standards govern text legibility, what are the WCAG 2.1 AA thresholds, and how does APCA differ?
expected_elements: WCAG 2.1 contrast ratio is computed from relative luminance
AA thresholds: 4.5:1 normal text, 3:1 large text (18pt+ or 14pt+ bold); AAA is 7:1 normal
APCA (WCAG 3 working draft) uses a perceptual model with Lc thresholds (e.g. 60 Lc body, 75 Lc small)
WCAG 2.1 remains the legally referenced standard in most jurisdictions; tooling can compute both

evals.prompt: How do you build a 10-step scale from a brand seed color and keep it perceptually even?
expected_elements: Anchor the brand color at a specific scale step (e.g. step 600) and generate the rest rather than hand-tuning
Generate in OKLCH/LCH so equal step indices have equal lightness (within ~±2 L units)
Export to sRGB or display-p3 with fallbacks for sRGB-only displays
Each step is derived by rule, not eyeballed individually

evals.prompt: How do semantic tokens let one token serve both a light and a dark theme while staying accessible?
expected_elements: A semantic token (e.g. text-primary) resolves to a different palette value per theme via the mapping layer
Example: near-black (L~0.15) on light, near-white (L~0.96) on dark — same component token
Both resolutions meet the same contrast requirement against their respective backgrounds
Tokens are named by intent / contrast pair (text-on-surface), never by appearance (text-dark-gray)

evals.prompt: A teammate asks the color-system-design skill to implement the prefers-color-scheme media query, persist the user's toggle, and prevent the theme flash on load. Is that in scope? Why or why not?
expected_elements: Not in scope — that is dark-mode-implementation (runtime detection, persistence, flash prevention, asset swapping)
color-system-design owns the palette and the contrast-correct token pairings the dark theme consumes
Correctly distinguishes owning what the colors ARE from owning how they are switched at runtime
May note theme-system-design owns token distribution/resolution architecture

evals.prompt: A stakeholder says 'a color system is just a nice set of swatches — any pleasant palette is a system.' Correct the mental model.
expected_elements: The swatches are the cheap part; the system is the perceptually-uniform scale generation, the intent-named semantic layer, and the contrast contract
A palette built by eye in sRGB/HSL gives uneven scales and silent contrast failures
Naming tokens by appearance in component code makes every brand refresh and theme a rewrite
Color as the only state signal excludes ~8% of men with color vision deficiency — pair with icon/text

evals.prompt: What would you check to verify a color system is implemented correctly?
expected_elements: Every text/background pair meets WCAG 2.1 AA, checked automatically in CI against token combinations
Scales generated in OKLCH/LCH; equal step indices within ±2 L units
Semantic tokens named by intent, not appearance, in component code
Every semantic token exists in both light and dark themes; color is never the sole state signal; palette previewed under protanopia/deuteranopia/tritanopia
